title: Śiva Goes Begging at His Own Door
tease: He has argued that the world is an illusion and food along with it. She turns the kitchens off. He lasts about a day, and then queues with a bowl.

source.traditionNote: The Kāśī Khaṇḍa establishes Annapūrṇā at Kāśī and has Śiva receive alms from her. The famous frame — the argument that food is māyā, and Pārvatī withdrawing until he is hungry — is how Kāśī itself tells the story and is not a verse you can point at. We tell the Kāśī version and say which part is the city's.
checkedAgainst: Skanda Purāṇa, Kāśī Khaṇḍa — Tagare trans. (Motilal Banarsidass)

variants.differs: Whether the argument about food is in the text at all
variants.tellings: The Kāśī Khaṇḍa gives Annapūrṇā feeding Kāśī and Śiva taking alms from her hand. The frame — that he called food māyā and she withdrew until he was hungry — is carried by the Kāśī temple tradition and the later Annapūrṇā literature rather than by a citable verse.
variants.weTell: The Kāśī version, with the join marked. Some stories live in a text and some live in a place.

variants.tellings: Some tellings have him praise her at length; others end at the bowl and say nothing more.
variants.weTell: The quiet ending, with what he said afterwards flagged as something only some tellings bother to report.

audience.careNote: A famine with food everywhere that will not feed anybody. And be ready for the real shape of it: she ends an argument by withholding food from a whole city until he gives in, and a child may well say that was too far. Nobody dies in the story. The two of them are not angry with each other, which is the strange part.

values: an argument nobody needed to have

blocks.text: «Śiva» often said that the world is «māyā»: real, but not always what it seems. We should not hold too tightly to the things in it.
«Pārvatī» let this run for a while. Then she asked him whether that included food.
He said it did. Obviously it did. Food is a thing in the world, and a man who has understood the world does not need it.
She said: _all right._ And she left.
Not in a temper, and not for long, but completely. What went with her was every part of the world that feeds anything.
Nothing ripened. The rice stood green and hard. Fruit hung and never came ready. Fires burned under pots, and whatever was in them was exactly as raw at the end as at the beginning.
So it was not a drought. There was food everywhere. It simply would not feed anybody.
«Kāśī» went hungry first, being her city and his. And after a while Śiva was hungry too, which he had not expected, having a whole position on the matter.
Soon even «Śiva» was hungry. He tried not to think about food, but he could think of almost nothing else.
Then somebody said there was a kitchen in Kāśī. She had set up in the middle of the city with a ladle and a pot that did not run out, and there was a queue, and everyone in it was being fed.
So he took his bowl and stood in the line. He had carried that begging bowl to more doors than anyone could count. He had never needed to bring it to his own.
She saw him coming and said nothing clever. She filled the bowl. Then she filled it again, because he was very hungry.
He had argued that nobody really needs feeding. He was the one who found out otherwise — in a queue, holding a bowl, at his own door.
This one starts with an argument in a house.
«Śiva» had been saying, for some time and to anyone who would sit still, that the world is «māyā».
Not that the world does not exist, but that it is not always what it seems, and that people should not cling too tightly to what is in it.
«Pārvatī» let this run for a while.
Then she asked him whether that included food.
He said it did. Obviously it did. Food is a thing in the world, the world is māyā, and a man who has properly understood that does not need it and should not want it.
He was not speaking carelessly. «Śiva» could sit on a mountain for ages without eating, so he believed he had tested the idea on himself.
She said: _all right._
And she left.
Not in a temper, and not for long, but completely. She took herself out of the world — and what went with her was every part of the world that feeds anything.
Nothing ripened. The rice stood in the fields and stayed green and hard. The fruit went on hanging and never came ready. Cows had milk in them and it would not come down.
And fires burned under pots, and the pots got hot, and whatever was in them was exactly as raw at the end as it had been at the beginning.
That is the detail people remember, because it tells you this was not a drought. There was food everywhere. It simply would not feed anybody.
«Kāśī» went hungry first, being her city and his.

It is the city he is said never to leave, and it went quiet the way a place goes quiet when everybody in it is thinking about the same thing. Every kitchen had become a reminder that food was present but useless.
After a while, «Śiva» was hungry too.
That surprised him. He had been very sure hunger did not matter.
Soon food was almost all he could think about.
Then somebody said there was a kitchen in Kāśī.

She had come back and set up in the middle of the city. There was a queue. She stood at the front with a ladle and a pot that did not run out, serving people one at a time. The same city that had gone hungry now had a kitchen again.
So he took his bowl and went and stood in the line, behind everyone else who had come because they were hungry.

Begging is his oldest job. «Bhikṣāṭana», they call him for it — the one who goes door to door with a bowl and takes whatever he is handed. He did not choose it; it was laid on him, long ago, as a penance for something he had done, and he had carried it to more doors than anybody could count.
He had never once had to do it at his own.
She saw him coming down the line and did not argue. She simply filled his bowl.
And then she filled it again, because he was very hungry.

What follows is less an apology than a correction: the world may be «māyā», but hunger still has to be answered. A hungry person in front of you is not an idea to debate. Whatever else is uncertain, the empty bowl in your hand is asking for something real.

She has been «Annapūrṇā» ever since, which means _full of food_. And Kāśī has never let the story go: it is why the city still insists nobody inside it should be hungry, and why there is a kitchen attached to her temple to this day.
He had been right that the world is not always what it looks like. He was still holding out the bowl when he stopped using that truth to talk past hunger.

linked.reason: the same goddess, considerably less patient

close.question: He had to hold out a bowl to someone in his own house. Has anyone ever had to help you with something you had said you did not need help with?
close.seed: Being fed by someone is not losing an argument.

ifTheyAsk.a: She was not, and the story is careful about it — she never taunts him, and she does not make him say he was wrong. But she did let a whole city go hungry to make a point, and it is fair to say so out loud. If your child thinks that was too far, they have noticed something real, and the story does not have a tidy answer for them.

Only about one thing. He is not wrong that the world is not what it looks like — that is a serious idea and the Purāṇas mean it. He is wrong that understanding it lets you skip the ordinary business of being fed. That is why he ends up in the queue and not in a debate.

ifTheyAsk.q: Is this actually in the book?
ifTheyAsk.a: Partly. The Kāśī Khaṇḍa has Annapūrṇā feeding Kāśī, and has Śiva take alms from her hand. The argument about food being an illusion, and her switching the kitchens off, is how Kāśī tells it rather than a verse anyone can point to — so we have told the city's version and labelled it. This is worth saying to a child: some stories live in a text, and some live in a place.
